Session consistency, which gives each user read-your-writes within their session.
Bounded staleness with a lag of one second behind the latest write.
questions.correct_rationale: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes within a client session with low latency and high availability, and it's the default for Cosmos DB. Strong adds latency and limits multi-region write scenarios, Eventual doesn't guarantee read-your-writes, and bounded staleness is stricter and costlier than needed.

questions.question: A global gaming company needs players on every continent to write game state to a database with single-digit-millisecond latency, and the service must continue accepting writes even if an entire region goes down. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure SQL Database with active geo-replication to the regions where players are overall.
Cosmos DB with multi-region writes and a conflict resolution policy in each region.
Cosmos DB with a single write region and read replicas in the other regions in Azure.
Azure Database for PostgreSQL with read replicas placed on each continent.
questions.correct_rationale: Cosmos DB multi-region writes let every region accept writes locally with low latency and remain writable during regional outages, with conflict resolution for concurrent updates.
questions.distractor_summary: SQL geo-replication and PostgreSQL replicas allow writes only on the primary, and a single write region adds latency for distant players.

questions.question: A new internal tool uses Cosmos DB with traffic that's intermittent: a few thousand operations per day with occasional short bursts, and long idle periods. The team wants to pay only for consumed request units without managing throughput. What should the architect recommend?
options: Provisioned throughput set at the level of the peak burst for the tool.
A dedicated gateway for the account to cache the intermittent requests.
Multi-region writes enabled so that the intermittent traffic is spread out overall.
Cosmos DB serverless, which bills only for the requests that the tool uses.
questions.correct_rationale: Serverless bills per request unit consumed and suits intermittent, low-traffic workloads without capacity planning.
questions.distractor_summary: Provisioning for peak wastes money, a dedicated gateway is a caching feature, and multi-region writes add cost for global needs the tool doesn't have.

questions.question: A company stores compliance archives in Azure Blob Storage. The data is almost never accessed, but when auditors request it, a delay of up to 15 hours is acceptable. The company wants the lowest storage cost. Which access tier should the architect recommend?
options: The Archive tier, which has the lowest storage cost for rarely read data.
The Cool tier, which suits data that is kept for at least thirty days overall.
The Cold tier, which suits data that is kept for at least ninety days overall.
The Hot tier, which keeps the data online with the lowest access cost overall.
questions.correct_rationale: The archive tier has the lowest storage cost and is offline, requiring rehydration that can take hours, which fits rarely accessed data with tolerant retrieval times.
questions.distractor_summary: Cool and cold tiers are online and cost more to store, and hot is for frequently accessed data.

questions.question: A media company's blob data is accessed frequently for the first 30 days, occasionally for the next five months, and rarely afterward, but must be kept for seven years. The company wants tiering to happen automatically. What should the architect recommend?
options: Move the blobs between the tiers by hand at the end of each quarter for the application.
Keep all of the data in the hot tier for the full seven years.
Use a lifecycle policy: cool at 30 days, archive at 180, and delete at seven years.
Store all of the data in the archive tier from the day it is uploaded in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: Lifecycle management rules automatically transition and delete blobs based on age or last access, optimizing cost.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual moves are error-prone, hot-only storage overpays, and archive-first makes early frequent access slow and expensive.

questions.question: A broker-dealer must store trade records in Azure Blob Storage in a non-erasable, non-rewritable format for six years to comply with SEC Rule 17a-4(f). Nobody, including account administrators, may delete or modify records before the retention period ends. What should the architect recommend?
options: Enable blob soft delete with a retention period of 365 days.
Apply immutable storage with a locked time-based retention policy of six years.
Place a resource lock on the storage account that holds the trade records overall.
Enable blob versioning so that earlier versions of the records are kept.
questions.correct_rationale: Locked time-based retention policies provide WORM protection that satisfies regulations like SEC 17a-4(f), preventing modification or deletion until retention expires.
questions.distractor_summary: Soft delete and versioning allow eventual deletion, and resource locks can be removed by administrators and don't protect blob data.

questions.question: A company's critical application data in a storage account must survive both a single availability zone failure and a full regional outage, and the application must be able to read data from the secondary region even before a failover is initiated. Which redundancy option should the architect recommend?
options: Locally redundant storage (LRS), which keeps copies within one datacenter.
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS), which keeps copies across zones in one region.
Geo-redundant storage (GRS), which copies to a paired region without zones.
Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS) with a readable secondary region.
questions.correct_rationale: RA-GZRS replicates across zones in the primary region and to a secondary region, with read access to the secondary at all times.
questions.distractor_summary: LRS and ZRS don't protect against regional outages, and GRS doesn't use zones in the primary or allow reads from the secondary without failover.

questions.question: A data engineering team is building a data lake for Spark and Synapse analytics. It needs directory-level operations such as atomic renames, and fine-grained POSIX-style access control on folders for different teams. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 with hierarchical namespace, using ACLs and Azure RBAC.
A standard blob storage account without the hierarchical namespace feature enabled overall.
Azure Files standard shares mounted by the Spark and Synapse clusters in every region.
Azure Table Storage, which holds the files as structured table entities in production.
questions.correct_rationale: Hierarchical namespace enables true directories with atomic operations and POSIX ACLs, optimized for analytics engines.
questions.distractor_summary: Flat blob namespaces lack efficient directory operations and ACLs, Azure Files isn't optimized for big data analytics, and Table Storage is for key-value data.

questions.question: A company is migrating SAP HANA and a high-performance Linux application that requires an NFS file system with sub-millisecond latency, very high throughput, and enterprise features such as snapshots and cross-region replication. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Files standard tier, with shares mounted over the SMB protocol.
Azure Blob Storage with NFS 3.0 enabled on a premium block blob account overall.
Azure NetApp Files, which provides high-performance NFS volumes for HANA.
Azure Table Storage, with tables mounted as file systems for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure NetApp Files provides high-performance, low-latency NFS and SMB volumes with snapshots and replication, and it's certified for SAP HANA. Standard Azure Files and blob NFS don't meet these performance characteristics, and Table Storage isn't a file system.

questions.question: A company with 60 branch offices wants to consolidate file servers into Azure while keeping fast local access to frequently used files at each branch, and users must continue using their Active Directory credentials and NTFS permissions. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Blob Storage, with a SAS token issued to each of the branch users overall.
Azure Files with AD DS authentication and Azure File Sync at each branch.
Azure NetApp Files deployed in every one of the sixty branch offices.
Email attachments in place of the shared file servers at each branch.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Files integrates with AD DS for identity-based access, and Azure File Sync caches hot files on branch servers while tiering cold data to Azure.
questions.distractor_summary: Blob SAS tokens lack NTFS permissions, NetApp Files isn't deployed in branches, and email isn't a file service.

questions.question: A company's storage accounts must not be reachable from the internet. Applications in Azure virtual networks and on-premises servers connected through ExpressRoute must access them using private IP addresses, with names resolving correctly from both environments. What should the architect recommend?
options: Service endpoints only, leaving public network access enabled on the accounts in every region.
Firewall rules that allow the on-premises public IP addresses to connect for the application.
Short-lived SAS tokens issued to the applications and the on-premises users for the application.
Private endpoints with public access disabled, plus Private DNS and on-premises forwarding.
questions.correct_rationale: Private endpoints give storage accounts private IPs in the virtual network, reachable over ExpressRoute, and private DNS integration ensures correct resolution from Azure and on-premises.
questions.distractor_summary: Service endpoints still use the public endpoint and don't extend to on-premises, IP firewall rules keep public exposure, and SAS doesn't control network access.

questions.question: A web application must give browsers temporary upload access to specific blob containers. Security prohibits distributing storage account keys and wants the delegated access tied to a Microsoft Entra identity so it can be audited and revoked. What should the architect recommend?
options: User delegation SAS tokens from the managed identity, scoped to the container and short-lived.
Account SAS tokens that are signed with the storage account key.
Make the containers public so that the browsers can upload the files throughout the organization.
Share the storage account key with the front end of the web application across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: User delegation SAS tokens are secured with Microsoft Entra credentials instead of account keys, supporting auditing and revocation of the delegation key.
questions.distractor_summary: Account-key SAS relies on keys, public containers are insecure, and sharing keys grants full account access.

questions.question: A company wants blobs in specific containers of a storage account in West Europe to be copied asynchronously to a storage account in North Europe to reduce read latency for a separate application and to keep an independent copy, without replicating the entire account. What should the architect recommend?
options: Geo-redundant storage for the whole storage account in West Europe.
A manual AzCopy job that the team runs once every week.
Object replication policies from the source to the destination for those containers.
Blob soft delete enabled on the containers that need the copies.
questions.correct_rationale: Object replication asynchronously copies blobs between containers in different storage accounts and regions, with independent destination accounts.
questions.distractor_summary: GRS replicates the whole account to a secondary that's not independently usable without failover, weekly AzCopy is stale and manual, and soft delete isn't replication.

questions.question: A database transaction log volume on an Azure VM requires sub-millisecond latency and the ability to adjust IOPS and throughput dynamically without detaching the disk. What disk type should the architect recommend?
options: A Standard HDD managed disk, which has the lowest cost per gigabyte for the application.
An Ultra Disk (or Premium SSD v2) configured with the required IOPS and throughput.
A Standard SSD managed disk, which is suited to light web workloads.
An Azure Files premium share mounted on the VM for the log volume.
questions.correct_rationale: Ultra Disk offers sub-millisecond latency and dynamically adjustable IOPS and throughput for demanding transactional workloads, and Premium SSD v2 also allows independent performance tuning.
questions.distractor_summary: Standard disks don't meet the latency requirements, and file shares aren't intended for database log volumes.

questions.question: A small internal application stores simple key-value records (device ID and a few attributes) totaling a few gigabytes, queried by partition key and row key. It doesn't need global distribution, secondary indexes, or low-latency SLAs, and cost must be minimal. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL with multi-region writes enabled for the records.
Azure SQL Database Business Critical for the simple key-value records.
Azure Cosmos DB for Table with dedicated throughput set for the records.
Azure Table Storage, a low-cost option for simple key-value records.
questions.correct_rationale: Table Storage provides inexpensive key-value storage suitable for simple access patterns without premium features.
questions.distractor_summary: Cosmos DB options add capabilities and cost that aren't needed, and Business Critical SQL is excessive.

questions.question: An application bug overwrote thousands of blobs with corrupted content, and a script accidentally deleted others. The company wants to be able to recover previous versions of overwritten blobs and restore deleted blobs for up to 30 days. What should the architect recommend?
options: Enable blob versioning and soft delete for blobs and containers with a retention period.
Enable geo-redundant storage so that a copy of every blob is kept elsewhere in production.
Apply a CanNotDelete lock on the storage account that holds the blobs for the application.
Move the blobs to the archive tier so that they cannot be overwritten for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Versioning keeps previous versions when blobs are overwritten, and soft delete retains deleted blobs and containers for a set period.
questions.distractor_summary: GRS replicates corruptions and deletions, resource locks don't protect data-plane operations on blobs, and access tiers don't provide recovery.

questions.question: A company needs to copy data nightly from on-premises SQL Server databases, which aren't reachable from the internet, into Azure Data Lake Storage, and orchestrate downstream transformations. It wants a managed, code-light integration service. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Logic Apps with the HTTP connector calling the on-premises servers.
AzCopy running on an administrator's laptop each night to copy the data.
Azure Data Factory pipelines with a self-hosted integration runtime on-premises.
Azure Event Grid events published from the on-premises SQL Server databases.
questions.correct_rationale: Data Factory orchestrates data movement and transformation, and the self-hosted integration runtime securely connects to on-premises sources.
questions.distractor_summary: Logic Apps isn't optimized for bulk data movement, a laptop-based copy isn't reliable, and Event Grid routes events rather than copying data.

questions.question: A company wants a unified SaaS analytics platform where data engineers use Spark, analysts use SQL, and business users use Power BI, all over a single copy of data in an open lakehouse format, with minimal infrastructure management. What should the architect recommend?
options: Separate Azure SQL databases that each of the teams manages for itself for the team.
Microsoft Fabric with OneLake, a lakehouse, a warehouse and Power BI experiences.
An HDInsight cluster that is provisioned separately for each of the teams in Azure.
Azure Table Storage with custom reporting built by each of the teams.
questions.correct_rationale: Microsoft Fabric provides integrated SaaS experiences for data engineering, warehousing, and BI over OneLake in open Delta format.
questions.distractor_summary: Separate SQL databases duplicate data, HDInsight clusters require management, and Table Storage isn't an analytics platform.

questions.question: A manufacturer streams millions of telemetry events per minute from factory sensors. It needs to detect anomalies with SQL-like queries over time windows in near real time and send results to a dashboard and a database. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Data Factory pipelines that are scheduled to run every hour.
Azure Queue Storage with a nightly batch job to process the events for the application.
Azure Blob Storage with Logic Apps triggered when new files arrive.
Event Hubs for ingestion with Stream Analytics windowed queries for the dashboard.
questions.correct_rationale: Event Hubs ingests high-volume event streams, and Stream Analytics performs real-time windowed queries with outputs to dashboards and databases.
questions.distractor_summary: Hourly or nightly batches aren't real time, and Blob Storage with Logic Apps isn't designed for high-throughput streaming analytics.

questions.question: An order service stores orders in Cosmos DB for NoSQL. Whenever an order is inserted or updated, several downstream systems (search index, notifications, analytics) must be updated in near real time, without adding logic to the order service's write path. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use the Cosmos DB change feed with Azure Functions to push changes downstream.
Poll the container every hour and look for the documents that have changed overall.
Have the order service call each downstream system synchronously on every write.
Export the container to Blob Storage each night for the downstream systems overall.
questions.correct_rationale: The change feed provides an ordered log of changes that functions or processors can consume to update downstream systems asynchronously.
questions.distractor_summary: Hourly polling is slow and inefficient, synchronous calls couple the write path to downstream availability, and nightly exports aren't near real time.

questions.question: A data science team needs a collaborative Apache Spark platform for large-scale data engineering and machine learning on Delta Lake tables, with notebooks, job orchestration, and integration with Azure Data Lake Storage. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure SQL Database with hyperscale compute for the Spark workloads overall.
Azure Stream Analytics jobs running the Spark code in the cloud.
Azure Databricks, a collaborative Apache Spark platform with notebooks.
Azure Functions with long timeouts running the data engineering code overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Databricks is a managed Spark platform with collaborative notebooks, Delta Lake, and ML capabilities integrated with Azure storage.
questions.distractor_summary: SQL Database isn't a Spark platform, Stream Analytics targets stream processing with SQL, and Functions aren't designed for large-scale distributed data processing.

questions.question: A research institute must move 600 TB of archived imaging data from its data center to Azure Blob Storage within five weeks. Its internet uplink is 300 Mbps and shared with other services. What should the architect recommend?
options: AzCopy running over the internet connection from the data center.
Azure Data Box devices, such as Data Box Heavy, shipped there and returned.
Azure Storage Mover running over the existing network link from the data center.
Azure File Sync with a server endpoint set up on the imaging file servers.
questions.correct_rationale: At 300 Mbps, transferring 600 TB online would take far longer than five weeks, so offline Data Box devices are appropriate.
questions.distractor_summary: AzCopy and Storage Mover are limited by the same link, and File Sync is for ongoing file share synchronization.

questions.question: Business analysts need to build data transformation logic (joins, aggregations, derived columns) on large datasets moved by Azure Data Factory, but they don't write Spark code. The company wants the transformations to run at scale on managed Spark. What should the architect recommend?
options: Stored procedures that run in an on-premises SQL Server for the analysts.
Azure Logic Apps workflows that the analysts build for each transformation.
Custom Python scripts that run on a VM and are maintained by the analysts.
Mapping data flows in Data Factory, a visual designer that runs on managed Spark.
questions.correct_rationale: Mapping data flows let users design transformations visually and execute them at scale on managed Spark.
questions.distractor_summary: On-premises stored procedures and VM scripts require code and infrastructure, and Logic Apps aren't built for large-scale data transformation.

questions.question: An operational application uses Cosmos DB for NoSQL. Analysts want near-real-time analytics on the operational data using Spark and SQL without building ETL pipelines and without consuming the request units provisioned for the transactional workload. What should the architect recommend?
options: Enable Synapse Link or Fabric mirroring so analytics use a separate analytical store.
Run the analytical queries directly against the transactional container in every region.
Export the data each night with Data Factory into a data warehouse for the application.
Increase the provisioned throughput of the container for the analytical queries overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Synapse Link and Fabric mirroring replicate Cosmos DB data into an analytical store automatically, enabling analytics without ETL and without affecting transactional RUs.
questions.distractor_summary: Querying the transactional container consumes RUs, nightly exports are stale, and extra throughput adds cost.

questions.question: Security requires that Azure Data Factory pipelines access Azure SQL Database, storage accounts, and Key Vault only over private connections, with no public network access enabled on those data stores. What should the architect recommend?
options: Allow all Azure services through the firewall of each of the data stores in every region.
Use the Azure integration runtime on the public network with IP allowlists in production.
Use an integration runtime in a managed virtual network with managed private endpoints.
Store the data in public containers so that the pipelines can reach it.
questions.correct_rationale: A managed virtual network with managed private endpoints lets Data Factory reach data stores privately, allowing public access to be disabled.
questions.distractor_summary: Allowing all Azure services and IP allowlists keep public exposure, and public containers are insecure.

questions.question: A retailer's 150 TB enterprise data warehouse runs complex analytical queries across billions of rows and needs massively parallel processing, workload isolation between reporting and data loading, and predictable performance. The workload has outgrown Azure SQL Database. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure SQL Database General Purpose with more vCores added for the queries.
An MPP warehouse, such as a Synapse dedicated SQL pool or Fabric warehouse.
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL with the data modeled for the analytical queries overall.
Azure Table Storage with the tables partitioned by date for each query.
questions.correct_rationale: MPP warehouses distribute data and queries across nodes for large-scale analytics and provide workload management for isolation.
questions.distractor_summary: Scaling up SQL Database has limits for this scale of analytics, and Cosmos DB and Table Storage are operational stores rather than warehouses.

questions.question: A company needs to back up Azure managed disks for a set of VMs using crash-consistent incremental snapshots, and also protect Azure Blob Storage containers and Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible servers, all managed through Azure Backup. Which vault type should the architect use for these workloads?
options: A Recovery Services vault that holds the disk backups for all of the VMs.
A storage account with lifecycle management rules applied to the disk snapshots.
A Backup vault, which supports incremental snapshot backups of managed disks.
Azure Site Recovery, which replicates the managed disks to a second region.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Backup uses Backup vaults for newer workloads such as Azure Disks, Blobs, PostgreSQL flexible servers, and AKS, while Recovery Services vaults handle workloads like Azure VMs, SQL in VMs, and Azure Files.
questions.distractor_summary: Lifecycle management doesn't provide backups, and Site Recovery is for replication and disaster recovery rather than backup.

questions.question: A company runs critical Azure VMs, including Trusted Launch VMs. The business requires an RPO of four hours for these VMs rather than the once-daily backup the team currently uses. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use an Enhanced backup policy in Azure Backup with backups every four hours.
Keep the Standard policy and take manual on-demand backups every four hours.
Use snapshots from a custom script rather than Azure Backup for the VMs.
Use Azure Site Recovery in place of backup for the critical VMs here.
questions.correct_rationale: The Enhanced policy supports multiple backups per day and is required for Trusted Launch VMs, meeting a four-hour RPO. Manual backups are error-prone, custom scripts lack management and retention features, and Site Recovery provides replication for DR rather than point-in-time backup retention.

questions.question: A company runs SQL Server on Azure VMs hosting business-critical databases. It needs an RPO of 15 minutes, point-in-time restore of individual databases, and centralized backup management without writing custom scripts. What should the architect recommend?
options: VM-level backups taken once each day for the SQL Server VMs.
Copies of the database files to Blob Storage that run every hour overall.
Azure Site Recovery replication on its own for the SQL Server VMs overall.
Azure Backup for SQL in Azure VMs, with log backups every 15 minutes.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Backup's workload-aware SQL backup supports log backups as often as every 15 minutes and point-in-time restore per database.
questions.distractor_summary: Daily VM backups miss the RPO, file copies aren't consistent backups, and Site Recovery doesn't provide point-in-time database restores.

questions.question: A manufacturer runs SAP HANA on Azure VMs. The SAP basis team requires backups integrated with SAP HANA's native backup interface, with log backups for point-in-time recovery and long-term retention, without managing backup infrastructure. What should the architect recommend?
options: Storage account snapshots of the OS disk of each of the HANA VMs.
Azure Backup for SAP HANA databases, which uses the Backint-certified integration.
Azure Files backup of the shares that store the HANA data files.
Manual copies of the HANA data files that the team makes each night in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Backup for SAP HANA uses the certified Backint interface for database-consistent backups, including logs, without backup servers.
questions.distractor_summary: OS disk snapshots aren't database-aware, Azure Files backup doesn't cover HANA databases, and manual copies aren't consistent.

questions.question: A company stores departmental data in dozens of Azure Files shares across subscriptions. Administrators create snapshots manually and often forget. The company wants scheduled backups with retention policies, centralized monitoring, and alerts. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure File Sync to on-premises servers that hold copies of the file shares.
Blob lifecycle management rules applied to the storage accounts for the shares.
Azure Backup for Azure Files with vault policies and Business Continuity Center monitoring.
Geo-redundant storage on the file shares, which holds a copy in a paired region.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Backup manages scheduled backups of Azure file shares with retention, centralized monitoring, and alerts.
questions.distractor_summary: File Sync isn't a backup solution, lifecycle rules apply to blobs, and redundancy replicates deletions or corruption instead of providing point-in-time recovery.

questions.question: A small company with a few on-premises Windows file servers wants to back up selected folders directly to Azure, with no backup server infrastructure and minimal cost. What should the architect recommend?
options: The MARS agent installed on each file server backing up to a Recovery Services vault.
Microsoft Azure Backup Server installed on a dedicated server for the file servers overall.
Azure Site Recovery replication of the file servers into the Azure region by default.
Azure Data Box shipments each month carrying the selected folders to Azure as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: The MARS agent backs up files and folders from Windows machines directly to Azure without an intermediate server.
questions.distractor_summary: Azure Backup Server requires additional infrastructure, Site Recovery replicates entire machines for DR, and Data Box is for bulk transfers.

questions.question: A company needs application-consistent backups of on-premises Hyper-V VMs, SQL Server, and SharePoint, with short-term local recovery copies on-premises and long-term retention in Azure. What should the architect recommend?
options: The MARS agent installed on each of the VMs and the application servers across the subscriptions.
Azure Site Recovery with recovery plans for the VMs and the SQL Server.
Blob Storage with AzCopy scripts that copy the application data each night for the application.
Azure Backup Server on-premises, with local backups offloaded to a Recovery Services vault.
questions.correct_rationale: MABS provides application-aware protection for workloads such as Hyper-V, SQL Server, and SharePoint, with local disk storage and offload to Azure for long-term retention.
questions.distractor_summary: MARS covers files and folders or system state, Site Recovery is for DR replication, and scripts don't provide application consistency.

questions.question: After a ransomware incident at a peer company, security wants to ensure that attackers who compromise an Azure backup administrator's account can't delete backups, shorten retention, or disable protection. What should the architect recommend?
options: Store the backups in locally redundant storage in the same region as the vault.
Use a locked immutable vault, keep soft delete, and require Resource Guard approval from another tenant.
Grant fewer users the Backup Contributor role and make no other change to it.
Take daily manual exports of the backups and keep them in another account.
questions.correct_rationale: Immutable vaults block operations that reduce protection, soft delete keeps deleted backups recoverable, and multi-user authorization requires approval from a separately controlled Resource Guard for critical operations.
questions.distractor_summary: Redundancy doesn't prevent deletion, fewer admins don't stop a compromised admin, and manual exports are impractical.

questions.question: A company backs up VMs to a geo-redundant Recovery Services vault in East US. During a prolonged East US outage, it must restore critical VMs into the paired region without waiting for Microsoft to declare a regional disaster. What should the architect have enabled?
options: Enable Cross Region Restore on the geo-redundant Recovery Services vault in East US.
Use locally redundant storage for the vault in East US and West US overall.
Use Azure Site Recovery for the backup items held in the vault in Azure.
Turn on blob versioning on the vault so the backups exist in West US overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross Region Restore lets customers restore backup data in the secondary region at any time from a geo-redundant vault.
questions.distractor_summary: LRS doesn't replicate to another region, Site Recovery is a separate replication service, and vault storage isn't managed through blob versioning.

questions.question: A team created a Recovery Services vault and began protecting VMs. Later, compliance required backup data to be stored in two regions, but the team found it couldn't change the vault's storage redundancy. What should the architect advise for future deployments?
options: Storage redundancy can be changed at any time, even after items are protected for the application.
Use LRS for all of the vaults to reduce the cost of the backups.
Rely on VM-level geo-replication instead of the vault's storage redundancy across the subscriptions.
Set the vault redundancy, such as GRS, before protecting items because it cannot change later.
questions.correct_rationale: Vault storage redundancy must be chosen before protecting any items; afterward, changing it requires a new vault.
questions.distractor_summary: It can't be changed freely, LRS doesn't meet two-region requirements, and VM replication isn't a substitute for backup storage requirements.

questions.question: A company protects thousands of items across 40 subscriptions using both Backup vaults and Recovery Services vaults, as well as Site Recovery. Operations wants a single place to view protection status, identify unprotected resources, monitor jobs, and manage policies at scale. What should the architect recommend?
options: Open each of the vaults individually in the portal and check them one by one.
Review the Azure Advisor recommendations for each of the forty subscriptions.
Use Azure Business Continuity Center for unified monitoring across vaults and subscriptions.
Use Azure Resource Graph queries only, since they list the vaults in each subscription.
questions.correct_rationale: Business Continuity Center provides a single experience to monitor and govern backup and DR across vault types and subscriptions, including finding unprotected resources.
questions.distractor_summary: Individual vault management doesn't scale, Advisor provides general recommendations, and Resource Graph alone lacks backup management actions.

questions.question: A company runs stateful applications on AKS with persistent volumes. It needs scheduled backups of cluster resources and persistent volumes, with the ability to restore specific namespaces to the same or a different cluster. What should the architect recommend?
options: Export the Kubernetes manifests from Git and keep nothing else for the clusters.
Azure Backup for AKS, using the backup extension together with a Backup vault.
Take VM backups of the AKS nodes and restore them to rebuild the cluster.
Use Azure Site Recovery on the AKS nodes to replicate the persistent volumes.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Backup for AKS captures cluster resources and persistent volumes and supports granular restore to the same or another cluster.
questions.distractor_summary: Git manifests don't include persistent data, node VM backups aren't a supported way to restore Kubernetes workloads, and Site Recovery doesn't protect AKS workloads.

questions.question: An application writes to block blobs in a storage account. A faulty deployment corrupted data across many containers over several hours. The company wants to be able to restore containers to their state at a specific time within the last 30 days, with minimal setup and no separate data copies. What should the architect recommend?
options: Move all of the blobs to the Archive tier so that they cannot be overwritten.
Use geo-redundant storage so a good copy of each blob exists elsewhere.
Place resource locks on the storage account to stop any further changes.
Use Azure Backup operational backup with point-in-time restore for block blobs.
questions.correct_rationale: Operational backup for blobs enables point-in-time restore of block blob data in the source account, using features such as versioning, change feed, and soft delete under the hood.
questions.distractor_summary: Archive and GRS don't provide point-in-time restore, and locks don't protect data-plane changes.

questions.question: A company uses Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, whose built-in backups support point-in-time restore for up to 35 days. Compliance requires retaining monthly backups for seven years. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use Azure Backup long-term retention for PostgreSQL flexible server, with a Backup vault.
Increase the built-in backup retention period of the server to seven years for the team.
Export the data to CSV files each month and store them in Blob Storage for the application.
Use a read replica of the server as a backup for the required period for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Backup provides long-term retention for PostgreSQL flexible server backups in a Backup vault, well beyond the built-in window.
questions.distractor_summary: Built-in retention is capped at 35 days, CSV exports aren't reliable backups, and replicas replicate deletions and corruption.

questions.question: A business owner says an order system can lose at most one hour of data and must be restored within four hours. How should the architect translate these requirements into a backup design?
options: Take backups every four hours and finish restoring the system within one hour.
Take full backups once each week and restore them whenever there is a need.
An RPO of one hour, needing hourly backups, and an RTO of four hours tested by restores.
An RPO of four hours, with backups every four hours, and an RTO of one hour.
questions.correct_rationale: RPO defines maximum data loss, which drives backup frequency, and RTO defines maximum time to restore, which the restore process must be tested against.
questions.distractor_summary: The other options misassign or ignore the requirements.

questions.question: A company runs a multi-tier application on Azure VMs in West Europe. It needs to recover the application in North Europe within one hour if West Europe fails, with an RPO of minutes, using a managed replication service. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Backup with Cross Region Restore to restore the VMs in North Europe.
Azure Site Recovery Azure-to-Azure replication to North Europe, with recovery plans.
Daily VM snapshots copied to North Europe and restored whenever there is an outage overall.
Geo-redundant storage on the VM disks so that a copy exists in North Europe as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Site Recovery continuously replicates VMs to another region with low RPO and orchestrated failover through recovery plans.
questions.distractor_summary: Backup restore takes longer and has a larger RPO, daily snapshots miss the RPO, and managed disks don't provide geo-redundant replication for VM failover.

questions.question: During DR drills, the team failed over database, application, and web VMs in random order, causing application errors because the application tier started before the database. The team also needs to run a script to update DNS and pause for a manual verification. What should the architect recommend?
options: Fail over all of the VMs at the same time and restart the services later.
Write a separate runbook outside Azure that lists the order of the failover for the team.
Fail over each VM by hand in the correct order during the drill.
Use a Site Recovery recovery plan with ordered groups and Automation runbooks for DNS.
questions.correct_rationale: Recovery plans define startup order through groups and support scripts and manual actions, making failover repeatable.
questions.distractor_summary: Simultaneous failover ignores dependencies, external runbooks aren't integrated, and manual failover is slow and error-prone.

questions.question: Auditors require quarterly proof that the Site Recovery DR plan works, but the business won't accept any disruption to production or replication during tests. What should the architect recommend?
options: Run a test failover to an isolated virtual network, validate the app, then clean up.
Perform a planned failover of the production workload every quarter for the auditors.
Stop the replication of the VMs during the test to protect the production data overall.
Test the plan only by reviewing the written documentation with the auditors overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Test failover creates VMs in an isolated network without affecting production or ongoing replication, enabling realistic validation.
questions.distractor_summary: Planned failover disrupts production, stopping replication creates risk, and documentation reviews don't prove recovery works.

questions.question: A company runs 300 VMware VMs on-premises and wants Azure as its disaster recovery site, with continuous replication, low RPO, and the ability to fail back to on-premises after an incident, without maintaining a second data center. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Backup with the MARS agent installed on each of the VMware VMs in every region.
Azure Data Box shipments each month carrying the VM disks to Azure.
Azure Site Recovery for VMware with a replication appliance, failover and failback.
Azure File Sync with the VM data copied to a cloud endpoint in Azure in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: Site Recovery replicates on-premises VMware VMs continuously to Azure and supports failover and failback.
questions.distractor_summary: MARS backs up files, Data Box shipments can't provide low RPO, and File Sync synchronizes file shares.

questions.question: A distributed application runs across five Azure VMs that write related data to their disks. After a Site Recovery failover, the VMs must be recovered to a common, consistent point in time so the application's data is consistent across machines. What should the architect configure?
options: Use separate replication policies for each VM with different recovery point settings.
A replication group in Site Recovery that provides multi-VM consistency for the five VMs.
Use Azure Backup for each of the VMs with the same schedule for all five of them.
Snapshots of the VM disks that are scheduled at different times of the day in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: Multi-VM consistency groups create shared crash-consistent and application-consistent recovery points across VMs.
questions.distractor_summary: Independent policies or snapshots produce inconsistent points in time, and backups don't provide continuous replication.

questions.question: A public web application runs on Azure App Service in East US with an Azure SQL Database backend. The business requires the site to remain available if East US fails, with automatic redirection of users to a secondary region. What should the architect recommend?
options: Increase the instance count of the App Service plan in East US for resilience.
Enable zone redundancy in East US only for the app and the database.
Back up the web app daily and restore it in West US if there is an outage.
Deploy a second app, use a SQL failover group, and route with Front Door health probes.
questions.correct_rationale: Multi-region deployment with Front Door health-based routing and a SQL failover group provides automatic regional failover for both tiers.
questions.distractor_summary: More instances or zone redundancy don't survive a regional outage, and restoring from backup is slow.

questions.question: A company must choose a DR approach for two applications. Application A has an RTO of 24 hours and tight budget constraints. Application B is revenue-critical with an RTO of under five minutes. What should the architect recommend?
options: A: backup or active-passive with minimal standby; B: active-active with global load balancing.
Active-active across two regions for both of the applications at the same time for the application.
Backup and restore for both of the applications, with each tested every year for the application.
No DR for Application A, and backup and restore for Application B throughout the organization overall.
questions.correct_rationale: DR strategies should match business requirements, using cheaper approaches for relaxed RTOs and active-active for near-zero RTOs.
questions.distractor_summary: Active-active for both overspends on A, backup and restore can't meet B's RTO, and leaving A unprotected ignores its RTO.

questions.question: A company's primary region is Germany West Central. Its data must remain in Germany, and it needs a secondary region for DR. The architect notices that some required services aren't available in every region. What should the architect consider when choosing the DR region?
options: Always choose the region closest to the headquarters, whatever the other constraints.
Always use the paired region, whatever the data residency and service availability.
Choose a region that meets residency and service needs, and plan for pairing limits.
Choose the cheapest region in the world as the secondary site for the company.
questions.correct_rationale: DR region selection must satisfy residency, service availability, and capacity, while understanding what depends on region pairs, such as geo-redundant replication targets.
questions.distractor_summary: Proximity or cost alone may violate residency, and pairing alone may not meet requirements.

questions.question: A company exposes a TCP-based (non-HTTP) API from VMs in two regions, each with its own public Standard Load Balancer. It wants clients to use a single DNS name that directs traffic to the primary region and fails over to the secondary region when the primary is unhealthy. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Front Door, which routes the TCP traffic to the closest healthy region.
Use Azure Traffic Manager with priority routing and endpoint monitoring for failover.
An Application Gateway in one region that sends traffic to both of the regions.
A single Standard Load Balancer that spans both of the regions in Azure.
questions.correct_rationale: Traffic Manager provides DNS-based routing for any protocol, and priority routing fails over to the secondary endpoint when health checks fail.
questions.distractor_summary: Front Door and Application Gateway are HTTP(S)-focused, and a regional Standard Load Balancer doesn't span regions.

questions.question: A company runs a microservices platform on a single AKS cluster in one region. The business now needs regional DR with an RTO of under 30 minutes. Application configuration is in Git, and state is stored in Azure SQL and Cosmos DB. What should the architect recommend?
options: Back up the node VMs and restore them in another region if there is an outage in production.
Increase the node count of the cluster so that it can absorb the failure for the application.
Enable availability zones on the existing cluster in its current region only in every region.
Deploy a second AKS cluster in another region with GitOps, replicated data and Front Door routing.
questions.correct_rationale: A second cluster deployed from the same GitOps configuration, geo-replicated data services, and global routing enable fast regional recovery.
questions.distractor_summary: Node VM backups aren't a valid AKS recovery method, and more nodes or zones don't survive a regional outage.

questions.question: A company uses GRS for a storage account in East US. During a prolonged regional outage, it wants to make the secondary region the new primary so that applications can write to the account again, without waiting for Microsoft. What should the architect recommend?
options: Start a customer-managed unplanned failover to the secondary region, accepting some data loss.
Change the account to LRS during the outage so that it stays available.
Create a new storage account and copy the data after the outage has ended.
Enable read access to the secondary only and keep waiting for the primary to return.
questions.correct_rationale: Customer-managed failover promotes the secondary to primary so writes can resume, with possible loss of recent data that wasn't replicated.
questions.distractor_summary: Converting to LRS doesn't restore availability, waiting prolongs the outage, and read access alone doesn't allow writes.

questions.question: A company's application stores secrets and certificates in Azure Key Vault in a region that has a paired region. The DR plan must ensure the application can read secrets after failover to the paired region. What should the architect know?
options: Key Vault data is lost whenever a regional outage occurs in the region.
Key Vault must be backed up manually every hour to remain available.
Vault contents replicate to the paired region and are read-only during failover.
Key Vault requires Azure Site Recovery to remain available in a regional outage.
questions.correct_rationale: Key Vault replicates to the paired region and offers read-only access during failover, which lets applications read secrets; separate vaults are needed for writes or non-paired DR regions.
questions.distractor_summary: Data isn't simply lost, hourly manual backups aren't required for this, and Site Recovery doesn't protect Key Vault.

questions.question: A business-critical application runs on two VMs in an availability set, which offers a 99.95% VM connectivity SLA. The business now requires a 99.99% SLA for the compute tier and protection against a datacenter-level failure within the region. What should the architect recommend?
options: Increase the availability set to five VMs to raise the SLA of the application.
Use a single VM with Premium SSD disks, which has a higher SLA than the set.
Move the VMs onto an Azure Dedicated Host to protect them from zone failures.
Deploy two or more VMs across availability zones in the region.
questions.correct_rationale: Deploying VMs across availability zones offers a 99.99% SLA and protects against the loss of a datacenter.
questions.distractor_summary: Availability sets protect against rack failures within a datacenter at 99.95%, a single VM has a lower SLA, and a Dedicated Host doesn't add zone resilience.

questions.question: A web application runs on Azure App Service in a single region. The business wants it to remain available if one availability zone fails, without deploying to a second region. What should the architect recommend?
options: Enable zone redundancy on a Premium v3 App Service plan with instances spread over zones.
Scale up the app to a larger instance size to absorb the failure of a zone.
Deploy two App Service plans in the same zone and balance traffic between them for the team.
Use deployment slots so that the app can be swapped when a zone fails.
questions.correct_rationale: Zone-redundant App Service plans spread instances across availability zones, keeping the app available if a zone fails.
questions.distractor_summary: Larger instances and plans in the same zone don't add zone resilience, and deployment slots are for staging releases.

questions.question: VMs in three availability zones run behind an internal load balancer. During a zone failure test, the load balancer's frontend IP became unavailable because it was pinned to the failed zone. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use a Basic Load Balancer, which supports availability zones for its frontend.
Assign the frontend to a single zone, the one that holds the most VMs in Azure.
Use a Standard Load Balancer with a zone-redundant frontend IP configuration.
Replace the load balancer with DNS round robin across the VMs in each zone overall.
questions.correct_rationale: A zone-redundant frontend on Standard Load Balancer is served from all zones and survives a single zone failure.
questions.distractor_summary: Basic Load Balancer doesn't support zones, a zonal frontend fails with its zone, and DNS round robin lacks health-aware failover.

questions.question: A company uses Application Gateway with WAF in front of a web tier spread across availability zones. The gateway itself must survive a zone failure and scale automatically with traffic. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use Application Gateway v1 with a fixed instance count spread across the zones.
Use Application Gateway v2 (WAF v2) across multiple zones with autoscaling.
Use a separate Application Gateway in each zone with DNS failover between them.
Use Azure Traffic Manager in place of Application Gateway for the web tier.
questions.correct_rationale: The v2 SKU supports zone redundancy and autoscaling, keeping the gateway available through a zone failure. v1 lacks zone support and autoscaling, per-zone gateways with DNS add complexity, and Traffic Manager doesn't provide WAF or Layer 7 features.

questions.question: A stateless web tier runs on a VM scale set in one zone. The team wants the scale set to spread instances evenly across three availability zones, continue running if one zone fails, and scale automatically. What should the architect recommend?
options: Run three separate scale sets in one zone each, and scale them manually.
Use an availability set with autoscale rules for the web tier VMs.
Use a single larger VM in one zone with a higher SLA than the scale set.
Use a zone-spanning scale set for zones 1, 2 and 3 with zone balancing and autoscale.
questions.correct_rationale: Zone-spanning scale sets distribute instances across zones with balancing and autoscaling, maintaining capacity during a zone failure.
questions.distractor_summary: Separate manual scale sets are harder to manage, availability sets don't span zones or autoscale, and a single VM has no redundancy.

questions.question: A solution consists of a web app with a 99.95% SLA that depends on an Azure SQL database with a 99.99% SLA. Both components are required for the solution to work. What is the approximate composite SLA, and what does it imply?
options: About 99.94%; the composite is lower than either part, so a higher target needs redundancy.
99.99%, which is the highest of the component SLAs in the solution.
99.95%, which is the lowest of the component SLAs in the solution.
About 99.99%, because the SQL database SLA covers the web app as well across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: For serially dependent components, SLAs multiply (0.9995 × 0.9999 ≈ 0.9994), so the composite SLA is below each component's SLA. Taking the highest or lowest component SLA misstates it, and adding SLAs is incorrect.

questions.question: A company uses Azure Service Bus Premium with the Geo-disaster recovery feature, pairing a primary namespace in East US with a secondary in West US. During a DR test, the team discovers that messages in the primary queues weren't available in the secondary namespace after failover. What should the architect explain and recommend?
options: Geo-disaster recovery replicates all messages, so the test must have been misconfigured overall.
Service Bus does not support any form of disaster recovery for its namespaces.
Geo-DR replicates metadata only, not messages; use geo-replication (Premium) for message data.
Enable zone redundancy, which replicates the messages across regions to the secondary as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Geo-disaster recovery replicates metadata only, so in-flight messages aren't copied; message-level replication requires the geo-replication feature or an application pattern such as sending to both namespaces.
questions.distractor_summary: Service Bus does support DR options, and zone redundancy protects within a region only.

questions.question: A clustered application uses a shared managed disk between two VMs in a single zone. The company wants the shared disk and cluster to remain available if that zone fails, with the VMs deployed in different zones. What should the architect recommend?
options: Locally redundant (LRS) managed disks shared between the two VMs in the zone overall.
Zone-redundant (ZRS) shared managed disks used by VMs deployed in different zones.
A Standard HDD disk attached to both VMs and replicated by the cluster software overall.
Daily snapshots of the shared disk, restored in another zone if the zone fails overall.
questions.correct_rationale: ZRS managed disks replicate synchronously across zones and can be attached to VMs in different zones, keeping the cluster available through a zone failure.
questions.distractor_summary: LRS disks are confined to one zone, HDD type doesn't add zone resilience, and snapshots don't provide continuous availability.

questions.question: A startup is building 15 containerized microservices. Some services are HTTP APIs and others process messages from Service Bus. The team wants scale to zero when idle, event-driven autoscaling based on queue length, built-in service-to-service communication patterns, and no Kubernetes cluster management. What should the architect recommend?
options: AKS with the cluster autoscaler enabled for all of the microservices.
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets running Docker containers on the VMs.
Azure Container Apps, with HTTP scaling and event-driven scaling and no cluster to manage.
Azure Batch pools, with each microservice submitted as a job to the pool.
questions.correct_rationale: Container Apps runs containerized microservices with scale to zero, KEDA-based event-driven scaling, and Dapr integration, without cluster management.
questions.distractor_summary: AKS requires cluster operations, scale sets with Docker require building orchestration, and Batch targets batch compute jobs.

questions.question: A platform team needs to run hundreds of containerized services with custom Kubernetes operators, custom admission controllers, a specific service mesh configuration, and fine-grained control over node pools and networking. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Kubernetes Service, which supports custom operators and full control of Kubernetes.
Azure Container Apps, which hides the Kubernetes API from the platform team.
Azure Container Instances, which runs single containers without orchestration for the team.
Azure App Service for Containers, which hosts web apps from container images in production.
questions.correct_rationale: AKS exposes the full Kubernetes API with control over node pools, networking, and custom extensions such as operators and admission controllers.
questions.distractor_summary: Container Apps abstracts the Kubernetes API, Container Instances runs individual container groups without orchestration, and App Service for Containers doesn't support Kubernetes operators.

questions.question: A data processing team needs to run short-lived containers on demand to process uploaded files, each running for a few minutes in isolation, and occasionally to burst additional Pods from an existing AKS cluster without adding nodes. The team wants per-second billing and no infrastructure management. What should the architect recommend?
options: A dedicated VM that is created for each uploaded file and then deleted.
Azure App Service with a web app that handles each upload in a request.
Azure Batch with a permanent pool that stays running between the file uploads overall.
Azure Container Instances, or AKS virtual nodes for bursting from the cluster.
questions.correct_rationale: Container Instances runs isolated containers quickly with per-second billing, and AKS virtual nodes use Container Instances to burst Pods without adding nodes.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-file VMs are slow and costly, App Service is for long-running web apps, and a permanent Batch pool incurs idle cost.

questions.question: A company is modernizing a .NET web application. It needs managed hosting with autoscaling, deployment slots for zero-downtime releases, managed TLS certificates, and integration with Microsoft Entra ID authentication, with minimal infrastructure work. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure VMs behind a load balancer, with scaling and patching run by the team overall.
Azure App Service, a managed host with autoscaling for .NET web applications.
Azure Container Instances running the application as one container with no scaling.
Azure Batch pools that host the web application on the pool nodes for the team.
questions.correct_rationale: App Service is a managed platform for web apps with autoscaling, deployment slots, managed certificates, and built-in authentication.
questions.distractor_summary: VMs require infrastructure management, Container Instances lacks slots and web platform features, and Batch is for batch processing.

questions.question: A company is building event-driven functions that process messages and must access databases through private endpoints in a virtual network. Traffic is bursty, with long idle periods. The company wants scale to zero when idle, fast scale-out during bursts, and the option to keep a few instances always ready. What Azure Functions hosting option should the architect recommend?
options: The legacy Consumption plan, which does not support virtual network integration overall.
A dedicated App Service plan that runs continuously at its largest size.
The Flex Consumption plan with virtual network integration and always-ready instances.
Azure Container Instances running the function host in a container group in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: The Flex Consumption plan combines serverless scale to zero with virtual network integration, fast scaling, and optional always-ready instances.
questions.distractor_summary: The legacy Consumption plan lacks VNet integration, a dedicated plan doesn't scale to zero, and Container Instances isn't a Functions hosting plan.

questions.question: An expense approval workflow must call several services in parallel (fan-out), aggregate the results (fan-in), then wait up to five days for a manager's approval before continuing, all in code with state managed automatically. What should the architect recommend?
options: Durable Functions orchestrations with activity functions and external events for approval.
A single HTTP-triggered function that is allowed to run for up to five days in every region.
A VM that runs a custom workflow engine for the expense approval process.
Azure Event Grid on its own, to fan out and wait for the approvals.
questions.correct_rationale: Durable Functions manage stateful orchestrations, including fan-out/fan-in and waiting for external events like approvals, without holding compute during waits.
questions.distractor_summary: A single function can't run for days, a custom engine adds overhead, and Event Grid routes events without orchestration state.

questions.question: A visual effects studio needs to render thousands of independent frames overnight. Jobs must be scheduled across hundreds of VMs, scaled automatically, and use low-cost interruptible capacity where possible, with the pool shrinking to zero when work is finished. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure App Service with many instances rendering one frame on each request.
The Azure Functions Consumption plan, with one function per frame to render.
A single large VM that renders the frames one after another overnight.
Azure Batch with autoscaling pools that use Spot VMs for the render jobs.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Batch schedules large parallel workloads across VM pools, autoscales them, and supports Spot VMs for cost savings.
questions.distractor_summary: App Service and Functions aren't built for heavy rendering, and a single VM can't finish thousands of frames overnight.

questions.question: A company runs stateless batch analytics jobs on VMs that can tolerate interruptions and restart from checkpoints. It wants to reduce compute costs as much as possible and is willing to accept that VMs may be reclaimed when Azure needs capacity. What should the architect recommend?
options: Three-year Reserved Instances for the VMs that run the batch analytics jobs.
Azure Spot VMs with a suitable eviction policy and a maximum price.
An Azure Dedicated Host that is used only for the batch analytics jobs.
Premium SSD v2 disks attached to standard VMs for the batch analytics jobs.
questions.correct_rationale: Spot VMs provide deep discounts for interruptible workloads, with configurable eviction policies and price caps.
questions.distractor_summary: Reservations suit steady workloads, Dedicated Host increases cost, and disk types don't reduce compute cost.

questions.question: A regulated company must run its Windows workloads on physical servers dedicated to its subscription, control the timing of host maintenance, and use existing per-core licenses that require dedicated hardware. What should the architect recommend?
options: Standard multi-tenant VMs, with data encryption turned on at the host for the team.
Azure Spot VMs, which run on spare capacity from the shared pool.
Azure Dedicated Host, which gives physical servers dedicated to the subscription.
Azure Container Apps, which run on a shared environment managed by Azure as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Dedicated Host provides physical servers dedicated to a single customer, with maintenance control and support for licensing scenarios requiring dedicated hardware.
questions.distractor_summary: Standard and Spot VMs run on shared hosts, and Container Apps doesn't meet these requirements.

questions.question: A company needs to provide 2,000 remote employees with Windows desktops and line-of-business apps from Azure. Most users can share multi-session hosts, user profiles must roam across sessions, and the company wants to use Microsoft 365 licenses where possible. What should the architect recommend?
options: One personal Azure VM for each employee, which stays running all day.
Remote Desktop Services deployed by hand on-premises for the employees.
VPN access for the employees to their desktops in the on-premises network for the application.
Azure Virtual Desktop with pooled multi-session hosts and FSLogix profiles on Azure Files.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Virtual Desktop with pooled multi-session hosts reduces cost, and FSLogix profile containers provide roaming profiles.
questions.distractor_summary: Personal VMs for everyone are costly, on-premises RDS doesn't move to Azure, and VPN to on-premises desktops doesn't meet the goal.

questions.question: A web tier must scale automatically across zones, mixing several VM sizes for capacity availability and combining a base of standard-priority VMs with additional Spot VMs to reduce cost. What should the architect recommend?
options: An availability set with VMs that the team creates and scales by hand for the team.
A Flexible orchestration scale set with several VM sizes and a Spot priority mix.
A single Dedicated Host group that holds the VMs for the web tier for the application.
Azure Container Instances groups created in each zone for the web tier for the team.
questions.correct_rationale: Flexible orchestration scale sets support multiple VM sizes, zone spreading, autoscaling, and mixing Spot and standard instances.
questions.distractor_summary: Availability sets don't autoscale, Dedicated Hosts increase cost, and Container Instances isn't a VM-based web tier.

questions.question: A company runs a steady set of production VMs 24/7 in a known region with stable sizes for the next three years. It also has variable compute usage across App Service, Azure Functions Premium, and different VM families that change often. It wants to reduce costs for both. What should the architect recommend?
options: Reservations for the stable VMs, and a compute savings plan for the variable usage.
Spot VMs for everything that runs in the production environment.
Pay-as-you-go pricing only, because it avoids any commitment to usage in every region.
A savings plan for the stable VMs only, with no discount for the other usage overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Reservations give the deepest discount for predictable, specific resources, while savings plans apply flexibly to variable compute across services and families.
questions.distractor_summary: Spot VMs aren't suitable for production steady state, pay-as-you-go forgoes discounts, and leaving variable compute undiscounted wastes savings.

questions.question: A company is migrating Windows Server and SQL Server workloads to Azure VMs and holds on-premises licenses with active Software Assurance. It wants to reduce Azure costs for these workloads. What should the architect recommend?
options: Buy new Windows and SQL Server licenses through Azure Marketplace for the VMs.
Use Spot VMs for the SQL Server workloads to lower the license cost.
Apply Azure Hybrid Benefit to the Windows Server and SQL Server VMs.
Run the workloads on Linux instead to avoid the license cost altogether.
questions.correct_rationale: Azure Hybrid Benefit lets eligible licenses with Software Assurance reduce Windows and SQL Server costs in Azure.
questions.distractor_summary: Buying new licenses duplicates spend, Spot VMs don't suit production databases, and switching operating systems isn't feasible for these workloads.

questions.question: A company deploys container images to AKS clusters in four regions. Image pulls across regions are slow and incur egress costs, and security requires that the registry be reachable only privately. What should the architect recommend?
options: Docker Hub public repositories pulled by the clusters in each of the regions in Azure.
Separate Basic registries in each region, with images copied across by hand.
Azure Blob Storage that holds the image layers for each of the regions.
An Azure Container Registry Premium registry, geo-replicated with private endpoints.
questions.correct_rationale: ACR Premium supports geo-replication for local pulls and private endpoints for private access.
questions.distractor_summary: Public repositories violate security, manual copying across Basic registries is error-prone and lacks private endpoints, and Blob Storage isn't a container registry.

questions.question: An AKS cluster runs critical system components and a mix of production APIs and interruptible batch jobs. The team wants system components isolated from application workloads, and batch jobs run on low-cost capacity that can be evicted, with node counts adjusting automatically. What should the architect recommend?
options: A single node pool for all of the workloads in the cluster.
A system pool, a user pool for production APIs and a Spot pool for batch jobs, autoscaled.
Separate AKS clusters for each type of workload that runs in the cluster for the application.
Run the batch jobs on the system node pool to save costs on the cluster for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Separate system and user node pools isolate critical components, and a Spot user pool with taints runs evictable batch jobs cheaply, with autoscaling adjusting capacity.
questions.distractor_summary: A single pool mixes workloads, separate clusters add overhead, and running batch on system nodes risks cluster stability.

questions.question: Applications running in AKS Pods need to read secrets from Azure Key Vault and write to Azure Storage. Security prohibits storing credentials in Kubernetes secrets or container images and wants each application to have its own identity. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use Entra Workload ID for AKS, federating Pod service accounts with managed identities.
Store a service principal secret in a Kubernetes secret that the Pods mount for the team.
Use the managed identity of the AKS node pool for all of the Pods in the cluster overall.
Hardcode the storage account keys in environment variables set on the Pods in production.
questions.correct_rationale: Workload ID federates Kubernetes service accounts with Microsoft Entra identities, giving each application its own identity without stored secrets.
questions.distractor_summary: Kubernetes secrets and hardcoded keys store credentials, and the node identity is shared by all Pods.

questions.question: An order processing system must process messages for each customer in the exact order they were sent, avoid processing duplicate messages that clients might resend, and support transactional operations across multiple messages. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Queue Storage, which delivers the messages in a roughly first-in order for the application.
Azure Event Grid, which pushes each event to the subscribers of the topic.
Service Bus queues with sessions keyed by customer ID, duplicate detection and transactions.
Azure Event Hubs with a single partition for all of the customers' messages for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Service Bus sessions provide ordered processing per session key, and Service Bus supports duplicate detection and transactions.
questions.distractor_summary: Queue Storage lacks ordering guarantees and transactions, Event Grid is for event routing, and a single Event Hubs partition limits throughput and doesn't offer duplicate detection or transactions.

questions.question: When a file is uploaded to a Blob Storage container, several independent handlers must react: a function that generates thumbnails, a Logic App that notifies users, and a webhook to an external system. The company wants push-based, near-real-time event delivery with filtering and retries, without polling. What should the architect recommend?
options: An Event Grid system topic on the storage account, with several filtered subscriptions.
A Service Bus queue that each of the handlers polls for the upload events.
A timer-triggered function that scans the container for new files every minute.
Azure Event Hubs with a consumer group for each of the handlers.
questions.correct_rationale: Event Grid delivers discrete events from Azure services to multiple subscribers with filtering and retry, using a push model.
questions.distractor_summary: Polling queues or timers adds latency and cost, and Event Hubs is designed for high-volume telemetry streaming.

questions.question: A connected-car platform ingests telemetry from 2 million vehicles, totaling millions of events per second. Multiple independent consumers (real-time analytics, archival, and anomaly detection) must read the same stream at their own pace. Existing producers use Kafka clients. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Service Bus topics, with one subscription for each of the consumers.
Azure Queue Storage, with one queue for the telemetry from each vehicle.
Azure Event Grid, with one subscription for each of the consumers of telemetry overall.
Event Hubs with partitions, a consumer group per consumer and the Kafka endpoint.
questions.correct_rationale: Event Hubs is built for massive event streams, with partitioned throughput, consumer groups for independent readers, and Kafka protocol support.
questions.distractor_summary: Service Bus and Queue Storage are for messaging rather than high-throughput streaming, and Event Grid targets discrete event routing.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform publishes order events. The shipping service needs only orders from the US, the fraud service needs orders above $1,000, and the analytics service needs all orders. Each service must receive its own copy of relevant messages reliably, even if it's temporarily offline. What should the architect recommend?
options: One Service Bus queue that is shared by all of the services for the events overall.
A Service Bus topic with a subscription per service, each using its own filter.
Azure Queue Storage with three queues that the producer writes to separately overall.
Direct HTTP calls from the order service to each of the consuming services.
questions.correct_rationale: Service Bus topics deliver copies of messages to multiple durable subscriptions, and filters let each subscription receive only relevant messages.
questions.distractor_summary: A shared queue delivers each message to only one consumer, producer-managed queues couple the producer to consumers, and direct HTTP calls fail when consumers are offline.

questions.question: A background processing system needs a simple, low-cost queue to buffer work items between a web front end and worker VMs. It doesn't need ordering guarantees, sessions, transactions, or pub/sub, but it may need to hold a very large backlog of messages accessible over HTTPS. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Service Bus Premium with sessions turned on for the work items overall.
Azure Event Hubs Dedicated, which is sized for very high event volumes.
Azure Queue Storage, a simple and low-cost queue in a storage account.
Azure Event Grid Namespaces with pull delivery for the work items overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Queue Storage is a simple, inexpensive queue that can hold very large backlogs limited by storage account capacity.
questions.distractor_summary: Service Bus Premium and Event Hubs Dedicated add unneeded features and cost, and Event Grid isn't designed as a simple work queue.

questions.question: A company exposes internal microservices as APIs to partners. It needs throttling and quotas per partner, API versioning, a developer portal, and transformation policies. Backend services must remain private in a virtual network, while partners access APIs over the internet through a WAF. What should the architect recommend?
options: API Management in internal VNet mode, fronted by Application Gateway with WAF.
Expose each microservice publicly with its own authentication and rate limits.
Azure Front Door routing directly to the backend services of the partners.
Azure Load Balancer with NAT rules that map the partner calls to services.
questions.correct_rationale: API Management provides throttling, versioning, developer portals, and policies, and internal VNet mode keeps it private while Application Gateway with WAF publishes it securely.
questions.distractor_summary: Public microservices lack central management, Front Door alone doesn't provide API management features, and a load balancer offers no API capabilities.

questions.question: A business operations team needs to automate a process that triggers when a new order appears in Salesforce, retrieves customer data from SAP, creates a record in Dynamics 365, and sends a Teams notification. The team prefers a low-code, visual designer with prebuilt connectors. What should the architect recommend?
options: Azure Functions with custom API clients written for each of the systems overall.
Azure Batch jobs that run on a schedule and poll each of the systems.
Azure Event Hubs, which receives the order events and sends them on to the systems.
Azure Logic Apps workflows that use prebuilt connectors for the systems.
questions.correct_rationale: Logic Apps provides a visual designer and hundreds of prebuilt connectors for SaaS and enterprise systems such as Salesforce, SAP, Dynamics 365, and Teams.
questions.distractor_summary: Functions require custom code, Batch is for compute-heavy jobs, and Event Hubs ingests event streams.
